summary: Describes the PPP Deflate protocol for compressing PPP packets. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP Deflate is a way to shrink the packets sent over a PPP link using the same deflate format as the gzip and zip programs. It needs both ends to keep the same record of what was sent, so every packet carries a counter. When the counter does not line up, the two ends throw that record away and start again.

subtitle: Compressing PPP packets with the deflate format, and coping with data that will not compress.

tldr.problem: A point-to-point link often carries repeated data, and compression only pays off if the two ends agree on what has already been sent.
tldr.mechanism: PPP Deflate uses the deflate compression format inside PPP packets, with a two byte sequence number on every packet so that a lost or reordered packet is noticed before the data is decoded.
tldr.outcome: Data that does not compress is sent in its original form, because deflate can add 14 to 18 bytes to a packet. The sequence number must then still be counted, or the two ends lose step.

today: RFC 1979 is an Informational memo from August 1996, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the deflate format and the zlib library, which the memo describes as freely available and widely used, and its own security considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: Introduction and Licensing
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) provides a standard method for transporting multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links, and the PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP) provides a method to negotiate and use compression protocols over PPP encapsulated links. This memo describes the use of the PPP Deflate compression protocol for compressing PPP encapsulated packets.

The deflate compression format, as used by the PKZIP and gzip compressors and as embodied in the freely and widely distributed zlib library, has four features that the memo lists. Its encoding and compression algorithm is apparently unencumbered, with an open and publicly available specification. It has a low-overhead escape mechanism for incompressible data, and the PPP Deflate specification offers options to reduce that overhead further. It has been heavily used for many years in networks, on modem and other point-to-point links, to transfer files for personal computers and workstations. And it easily achieves 2:1 compression on the Calgary corpus using less than 64KBytes of memory on both sender and receiver.

The zlib source is widely and freely available, subject to a copyright notice and three conditions. The origin of the software must not be misrepresented, so nobody may claim to have written the original software. Altered source versions must be plainly marked as such. And the notice may not be removed or altered from any source distribution. The deflate format and compression algorithm are based on Lempel-Ziv LZ77 compression, and extensive research by the GNU Project and the Portable Network Graphics working group supports its patent free status.
sections.plainLanguage: The format itself is not new. It is the same one behind gzip and zip, which is why the memo could point at existing, widely used software instead of inventing something.

sections.title: PPP Deflate Packets, Reliability and Expansion
sections.content:
Before any PPP Deflate packets may be communicated, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the CCP Control Protocol must reach the Opened state. Exactly one PPP Deflate datagram is encapsulated in the PPP Information field, where the PPP Protocol field contains 0xFD or 0xFB. 0xFD is used when the PPP multilink protocol is not used, or is used above multilink. 0xFB is used below multilink, to compress independently on individual links of a multilink bundle. The maximum length of the PPP Deflate datagram sent over a PPP link is the same as the maximum length of the Information field of a PPP encapsulated packet. Only packets with PPP Protocol numbers in the range 0x0000 to 0x3FFF, and neither 0xFD nor 0xFB, are compressed; other PPP packets are always sent uncompressed, because control packets are infrequent and should not be compressed for robustness. PPP Deflate packets require the previous negotiation of the Self-Describing-Padding Configuration Option if padding is added to packets.

PPP Deflate requires packets to be delivered in sequence. It relies on Reset-Request and Reset-Ack LCP packets, or on renegotiation of the Compression Control Protocol, to indicate loss of synchronization between the transmitter and receiver. The LCP FCS detects corrupted packets and the normal mechanisms discard them, and missing or out of order packets are detected by the sequence number in each packet, which ought to be checked before the packet is decoded. Instead of transmitting a Reset-Request when it detects a sequence error, the receiver may force CCP to drop out of the Opened state by transmitting a new CCP Configure-Request, though that method is more expensive than using Reset-Requests.

When the receiver first encounters an unexpected sequence number it should send a Reset-Request. When the transmitter sends the Reset-Ack, or the receiver receives it, both must reset the sequence number to zero, clear the compression dictionary, and resume sending and receiving compressed packets. The receiver must discard all compressed packets after detecting an error and until it receives a Reset-Ack, which the memo describes as abandoning the transmission of one file and starting the transmission of a new one. The transmitter must clear its compression history and respond with a Reset-Ack each time it receives a Reset-Request, because it cannot know whether previous Reset-Acks reached the receiver. The receiver need not do anything to its history when it receives a Reset-Ack, because deflate is a sliding-window compressor and the transmitter will simply not refer to any prior history.

Deflate expands incompressible data by approximately 14 to 18 bytes: 8 bytes at worst case at the deflate level, 2 further bytes for the deflate end-of-block and the zero-length synchronization block header, 2 bytes of sequence number, and 2 bytes to account for adding the PPP Protocol field to the transmitted data unit. If an incompressible data packet does not fit within the MRU of the link, the packet must be sent in its original form without CCP encapsulation, and PPP packets with significant data expansion that do fit should also be sent in their original form. In both cases the transmitter must increment the sequence number, because future encapsulated packets depend on the correct reception of some number of unencapsulated packets. When a PPP packet is received with PPP Protocol numbers in the range 0x0000 to 0x3FFF, other than 0xFD and 0xFB, it is assumed that the packet would have caused expansion, and the packet is locally added to the compression history. Sending incompressible packets in their native encapsulation avoids maximum transmission unit complications, but it complicates the implementation, because the transmitter and the receiver must start putting information into the compression dictionary with the same packets, without relying on seeing a compressed packet for synchronization.
sections.plainLanguage: Data that will not shrink is a problem, because the compressed form can be bigger than the original. The memo's answer is to send that data untouched, but to keep counting it in the sequence number so both ends still agree on what has been sent.

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
The PPP Deflate packet holds a PPP Protocol field and a Sequence field, then the Data. When the compression protocol has been successfully negotiated by the Compression Control Protocol, the value of the protocol field is 0xFD or 0xFB, and that value may itself be compressed when Protocol-Field-Compression is negotiated.

The sequence number is sent most significant octet first. It starts at 0 when the dictionary is cleared, and is incremented by 1 for each packet, including uncompressed packets; after 65535 it is zero again, so it wraps in the usual way. Its purpose is to ensure that lost or out of order packets do not cause the compression databases of the peers to become unsynchronized. When an unexpected sequence number is encountered, the dictionaries must be resynchronized with a CCP Reset-Request or Configure-Request, and the packet sequence number can be checked before a compressed packet is decoded.

The Data field holds the compressed PPP encapsulated packet, that is the Protocol and Data fields of the original uncompressed packet. Protocol field compression must be applied to the protocol field of the original packet before the sequence number is computed or the entire packet is compressed, regardless of whether PPP protocol field compression has been negotiated, so if the original protocol number was less than 0x100 it must be compressed to a single byte. The basic format of the compressed data is described by the deflate compressed data format specification. Each transmitted packet must begin at a deflate block boundary, to keep synchronization when incompressible data resets the transmitter's state, and to achieve that each transmitted packet must be terminated with a zero-length deflate non-compressed block, with a BTYPE of 00. The last four bytes of the compressed format must therefore be 0x00 0x00 0xFF 0xFF, and these bytes must be removed before transmission; the receiver can reinsert them if the implementation requires it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a two byte counter, and the compressed data always ends with the same four bytes so that the receiver knows where the next packet starts.

sections.title: Configuration Option Format
sections.content:
The CCP PPP Deflate Configuration Option negotiates the use of PPP Deflate on the link. By default, or on ultimate disagreement, no compression is used. The option has a Type of 26 and a Length of 3, followed by a Window field, a Method field, an MBZ field and a Chk field.

The Window field represents the maximum window size the decompressor is willing to allocate, expressed as the base-2 logarithm of the LZ77 window size minus 8. A deflate compliant decompressor must be willing to accept the maximum 32KB window size, represented by a value of 7. A deflate compliant compressor is at liberty to use a reduced window size, so a PPP Deflate compressor must either honor the restriction requested or reject the option. The Method field must be the binary number 1000, which represents the zlib compression method identifier of 8 for deflate compression with up to a 32K window size. The MBZ field must be all 0 bits, and the Chk field must be 00 to specify the sequence number check method.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree on one thing that matters: how much history the decompressor is willing to hold. Everything else in the option is fixed.
